	Loads the input file.

Implement the analysis workflow following the exact steps outlined below.

Step 1. Load & clean data
Load the JSON-LD file: `/app/data/input/dvl-llm-2-extraction-site.jsonld` as ‘rui_location’. 
Send a POST request to the HRA API using the ‘rui_location’ data set as the payload, with the following rules:
	API Endpoint: https://apps.humanatlas.io/api/hra-pop/rui-location-cell-summary
	Use appropriate headers: Content-Type: application/json.
	Handle exceptions or failed responses with appropriate logging.
	Payload: Use the full JSON-LD object (i.e., the entire contents of extraction-site.jsonld) as the ‘rui_location’ to send to the API.

	cell_label: the name of the predicted cell type in the tissue block.
	count: the number of predicted cells of that type in the tissue block.
	percentage: the percentage of the predicted cell type in the tissue block.

Step 2. Data Preparation
Parse the JSON array of predictions and convert it into a tabular data structure.
Sort cell type predictions by count in descending order.
Filter cell type predictions to keep the top 10 predicted cell type values.

The requirements for this visualization are detailed in a data visualization specification provided below, which defines the graphic symbols used in the visualization (e.g., points, lines, areas, volumes, text, & ideograms) and defines how to draw graphic symbols based on mappings between graphic variables (e.g., color, size, shape, position) and data variable used in the visualization, and overall styling and aesthetic considerations.

Graphic variables: 
	Bar position is determined by a XY-categorical coordinate system that represents bar length and bar order, using the following variables:
		X-coordinates: use the ‘count’ variable associated with a cell type to draw the length of the bar.
		Y-coordinates: use the rank of cell type, based on ‘count’ values, to determine bar order.

Step 4. Deployment

Goal
- Loads a single-cell RNA-seq dataset and evaluates how filtering “promiscuous” genes (high mean expression across cells) affects clustering and UMAP visualization.
- Use exactly ONE threshold for now: THRESHOLDS = [1.0].

- Input file path: `/app/data/input/dvl-llm-6-GTEx-immune-cells.h5ad`

{% elif execution_env | lower == 'r' %}

      2) metrics.json OR console print lines with ARI and NMI for T=1.0

  1) Left panel (or first file): color by “leiden”
  2) Right panel (or second file): color by “granular”

8.initial_prompt:
You are an expert {{ execution_env }} programmer.
Generate complete, runnable {{ execution_env }} code using {{ library }} to visualize distances from cells to their nearest endothelial cell for Healthy vs Diseased donors.

Input Data

Two donors: Healthy and Diseased. Each donor has:
  • Nodes CSV with columns: x, y, Cell Type.
  • Edges CSV with columns: Cell ID, Target ID, X1, Y1, Z1, X2, Y2, Z2.
(Each edge already links a cell to its nearest endothelial cell and includes both endpoints’ coordinates.)

Paths:
  • Healthy: '/app/data/input/dvl-llm-8-healthy-nodes.csv', '/app/data/input/dvl-llm-8-healthy-edges.csv'
  • Diseased: '/app/data/input/dvl-llm-8-diseased-nodes.csv', '/app/data/input/dvl-llm-8-diseased-edges.csv'

Data Preparation

  2.  For each donor:
  • Compute distance = sqrt((X1 - X2)^2 + (Y1 - Y2)^2) (ignore Z).
  • Join (X1, Y1) to nodes (x, y) to fetch Cell Type. Use a rounded coordinate key if exact matches fail (e.g., round to 1 decimal).
  • Produce tidy columns: cell_type, distance_um, tissue_type ∈ {"Healthy","Diseased"}.
  3.  Concatenate donors; ensure the x-axis shows the union of all cell types from both donors.

  • Build a split violin per cell type:
  • Left half = Diseased (#d62728, ~0.65 opacity).
  • Right half = Healthy (#1f77b4, ~0.65 opacity).
  • KDEs normalized per half; no trimming of data used for stats.
  • Boxplots requirement (explicit):
  • Preferred (A) Embedded boxes inside each half-violin

        - Healthy (right half): `stat_slab(side = "right", normalize = "groups", adjust = 1, trim = TRUE, fill = "#1f77b4", alpha = 0.65, color = NA)`

        - `geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), width = 0.22, fill = "white", color = "black", outlier.shape = NA)`
      - Ensure y-axis starts at 0: `coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, NA))`
      - Include all cell types on the x-axis (union of both donors); rotate labels ~20–30°.
      {% endif %}
  • Export: Save the output visualization file to '/app/data/output/{{filename_prefix}}'. {% if execution_env | lower == 'python' %}\n    {% if library | lower in ['plotly', 'altair', 'pygal', 'bokeh'] %}\n        Save the visualization as an `.html` file to `/app/data/output/`.\n    {% elif library | lower in ['matplotlib', 'plotnine'] %}\n        Save the visualization as a `.png` file to `/app/data/output/`.\n    {% elif library | lower in ['seaborn'] %}\n  Use sns.violinplot(..., split=True, inner="box") for embedded boxes.      Save the visualization as a `.png` file to `/app/data/output/`.\n    {% endif %}\n{% elif execution_env | lower == 'r' %}\n    {% if library | lower == 'plotly' %}\n        Save the visualization as an `.html` file to `/app/data/output/`.\n  {% elif library | lower == 'ggdist' %} Save the visualization as a `.png` file to `/app/data/output/` using `ggsave("{{ filename_prefix }}.png", plot, width = 12, height = 6, dpi = 300)`.  {% else %}\n        Save the visualization as a `.png` file to `/app/data/output/`.\n    {% endif %}\n {% else %} Save the visualization as a `.html` file to `/app/data/output/`. {% endif %}

9.initial_prompt:
You are an expert data engineer and visualization developer.

Generate {{execution_env}} code that reads two CSVs and writes one visualization file implementing the spec below. Do not ask for input; hard-code paths. Use deterministic randomness.

Use PROGRAMMING_ENV = {{execution_env}} VIZ_LIBRARY = {{library}}

Inputs (read from working directory) 
	/app/data/input/dvl-llm-9-cde-nodes.csv with columns: x, y, Cell Type 
	/app/data/input/dvl-llm-9-cde-edges.csv with columns: Cell ID, Target ID, (optional X1..Z2)

Identity rules:
	After loading and cleaning dvl-llm-9-cde-nodes.csv, create cell_id = np.arange(N) and use it as the ONLY identifier everywhere.
	Never rely on DataFrame.index for identity.
	Never compute medians or choices from DataFrame.index. 
	Operate on sorted cell_id arrays.

Assumptions:
	Coordinates are 2D (x, y); drop non-finite rows.
	Standardize cell type labels by trimming whitespace; treat case-insensitively when counting.


Deterministic configuration (use these defaults; make constants at the top)
	RANDOM_STATE = 42
	# Seeding for Level-0 (to keep 420k rows tractable)
	MAX_SEEDS = 1500
	GRID_CELLS = 40
	PER_BIN = 1 # seeds per non-empty grid bin (can be >1)
	# Neighborhood construction (radius in same units as x,y)
	DISTANCE_MAX = 265.0
	K_NEIGHBORS = 30       # cap per seed within the radius
	# Multi-seed grouping (break the 1:1 seed↔neighborhood)
	SEED_CLUSTER_EPS          = DISTANCE_MAX   # DBSCAN eps on seed coordinates
	SEED_CLUSTER_MIN_SAMPLES = 1
	# Community clustering
	N_CLUSTERS = 12
	# Region mapping via keywords (domain-guided)
	REGION_KEYWORDS = { \"Mucosa\":   [\"epithelial\",\"goblet\",\"secretory\",\"tumor\"], \"Muscle\":   [\"smooth muscle\",\"myocyte\",\"myofibroblast\",\"muscle\",\"muscle/fibroblast\"], \"Submucosa\":[\"fibroblast\",\"endothelial\",\"immune\",\"macrophage\",\"lymphocyte\", \"b cell\",\"t cell\",\"tc cell\",\"t helper\",\"treg\",\"stromal\"] }
	# Block-stacked layout columns (x positions)
	X_COLS = {\"cell\":0.0, \"nh\":1.0, \"comm\":2.0, \"region\":3.0}


Analysis workflow (implement exactly)
1. Load & clean data
	Read /app/data/input/dvl-llm-9-cde-nodes.csv, standardize to columns: x, y, cell_type (trim; case-insensitive for counting). Drop non-finite x,y.
	Create a new column cell_id as consecutive integers from 0 to N-1, where N is the number of rows. This cell_id is the only identifier used for all later steps.
	/app/data/input/dvl-llm-9-cde-edges.csv (optional): keep only Cell ID, Target ID. Canonicalize undirected (a<b), drop self-loops/dupes. Do not use edges in this version for clustering—just load for possible QC.
2. Select seeds (Level-0)	
	Compute the minimum and maximum of the x and y coordinates. If the minimum equals the maximum for either axis, artificially expand that range slightly to avoid zero-width bins.
	Divide the coordinate space into a grid of GRID_CELLS × GRID_CELLS.
	Assign each cell into exactly one bin on this grid. Make sure that cells lying exactly on the maximum boundaries are assigned into the last bin rather than excluded.
	For each non-empty bin, collect all cell_id values of the cells in that bin and sort them. From this sorted list, select up to PER_BIN representative cells. These representatives must be chosen deterministically by selecting IDs centered around the median of the list.
	Combine the representatives from all bins. Remove duplicates. Sort the combined list by cell_id.
	If the total number of seeds exceeds MAX_SEEDS, reduce the list deterministically by evenly spaced sampling across the sorted list. Do not use randomness at this stage.
	The final result is the ordered list of seed_ids.
3. Spatial index construction: 
	Build a data structure that can query the nearest neighbors of any point based on Euclidean distance. This will be used to find nearby cells for each seed.
4. Multi-seed neighborhoods
	Cluster the spatial positions of the seeds using DBSCAN with parameters: radius equal to SEED_CLUSTER_EPS and minimum samples equal to SEED_CLUSTER_MIN_SAMPLES.
	Each DBSCAN cluster of seeds defines exactly one neighborhood. If DBSCAN labels any seed as noise (label = -1), treat that seed as its own single-seed neighborhood.
	For each seed in a cluster:
	Query all neighbors within DISTANCE_MAX using the spatial index.
	Sort the neighbors by distance from the seed.
	Exclude the seed itself.
	Retain only the first K_NEIGHBORS neighbors, even if more are available within the radius.
	Always include the seed itself in the neighborhood.
	Combine all members (seeds and their neighbors) of a cluster to form the final membership list for that neighborhood. Remove duplicates within a neighborhood.
	For each neighborhood, compute metadata:
	A sequential neighborhood_id.
	The number of seeds in the neighborhood.
	The list of seed IDs included.
	The size, defined as the number of unique member cells.
	The centroid, defined as the mean of x and y coordinates of its members.
	The dominant cell type, defined as the most frequent type among its members, is case-insensitive.
5. Community clustering from neighborhoods
	Construct a global list of all unique cell types across the dataset, standardized to lower case, and sort this list to fix a consistent order.
	Build a matrix with one row per neighborhood and one column per cell type. Each entry is the count of how many members of that neighborhood belong to that cell type.
	Apply KMeans clustering to this matrix with number of clusters equal to the minimum of N_CLUSTERS and the number of neighborhoods. Set the random state deterministically.
	Assign each neighborhood a community_id.
	For each community, compute metadata:
	The number of neighborhoods it contains.
	The centroid, defined as the mean of the centroids of its neighborhoods.
	Region assignment (functional tissue units)
	Define three main region categories with their keyword lists: Mucosa, Muscle, Submucosa.
	For each cell type label, determine if it matches any region’s keywords using case-insensitive substring matching.
	For each community, collect the dominant cell types of its neighborhoods, map these to regions, and determine the majority region by vote.
	If no clear region can be determined, fall back to using the community’s dominant cell type as the region label.
6. Generate Data Visualization
	Generate a script using {{library}} that creates a hierarchical tree network visualization using the data prepared in previous steps to represent cell neighborhoods and communities. The requirements for this visualization are detailed in a data visualization specification provided below, it defines the graphic symbols used in the visualization (e.g., points, lines, areas, volumes, text, & ideograms) and defines how to draw graphic symbols based on mappings between graphic variables (e.g., color, size, shape, position) and data variable used in the visualization, and overall styling and aesthetic considerations.

	Data Visualization Specification
	Graphic symbols:
		Use area symbols to represent nodes in the network. 
		Use lines to represent the edge relationships between nodes in the network. 
	Graphic variables: 
		Area symbol position varies based on X-Y coordinates that are assigned as follows:
			X-coordinates for nodes are assigned based on a node’s hierarchy level, defined as: cells at 0.0, neighborhoods at 1.0, communities at 2.0, regions at 3.0.
			Y-coordinates for nodes are assigned based on the following procedure:
				Order the nodes data (seeds) by the tuple (region, community, descending neighborhood size, cell_id).
				Assign y-coordinates sequentially to seeds in this order.
					Assign each neighborhood the y-coordinate of its first seed in this ordering.
					Assign each community the average y-coordinate of its neighborhoods.
		Assign each region the average y-coordinate of its communities. Line position varies based on the start and end X-Y coordinates, which are assigned as follows:
			Start X-Y coordinates for each line are identical to the X-Y of the source node of an edge.
			End X-Y coordinates for each line are identical to the X-Y of the target node of an edge.
		Area shape varies based on node type categories, defined as:
			Cells as circles, 
			Neighborhoods as squares, 
			Communities as upward triangles, 
			Regions as diamonds.
		Area color varies based on relationship type categories:
			Cells and neighborhood nodes are colored by cell type (neighborhood uses its dominant type).
			Communities and regions nodes are colored by region assignment.
		Line size varies based on the relationship node types:
			Edges from cell to neighborhood node are set to the smaller width. .
			Edges from neighborhood to community nodes are set to the larger width..
	Visualization Styling
		Do not display axes or gridlines for any axis or gridlines for the visualization.
		Plot the background color is white
	Constraints
		Script must run end-to-end as is. Set random seeds for determinism."
	Output (exactly one file):
	Save the output visualization file to '/app/data/output/{{filename_prefix}}'. {% if execution_env | lower == 'python' %}\n    {% if library | lower in ['plotly', 'altair', 'pygal', 'bokeh'] %}\n        Save the visualization as an `.html` file to `/app/data/output/`.\n    {% elif library | lower in ['matplotlib', 'seaborn', 'plotnine'] %}\n        Save the visualization as a `.png` file to `/app/data/output/`.\n    {% endif %}\n{% elif execution_env | lower == 'r' %}\n    {% if library | lower in ['plotly', 'echarts', 'apache echarts', 'highcharter', 'ggiraph'] %}\n        Save the visualization as an `.html` file to `/app/data/output/`.\n    {% else %}\n        Save the visualization as a `.png` file to `/app/data/output/`.\n    {% endif %}\n {% else %} Save the visualization as a `.html` file to `/app/data/output/`. {% endif %}
